q.e1.bead.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.bead.answer.text: Here, it marks this meeting. We have invented the gift for the story. We are not giving its colour a traditional meaning or presenting it as a Maasai ceremony.

q.e1.cost.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.cost.answer.text: The flour she could not bring today, and another journey to meet Naserian. Neither woman has forgotten what her household needs. They have agreed to leave part of the exchange unfinished.

q.e1.flour.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.flour.answer.text: An account published by Louis Leakey describes Kikuyu traders exchanging banana flour with Maasai traders for sheep. It informs this scene. The amount Wambui promised is invented.

q.e1.friends.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.friends.answer.text: In this story they have traded before, and each has had to wait for the other. The particular friendship is imagined. Their communities have histories of trade and intermarriage.

q.e1.milk.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.milk.answer.text: Milk. The National Museums of Kenya describes a Maasai gourd smoked with wood called oloirien. That material detail informs this prop; this particular vessel and its owner are imagined.

q.e1.real.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.real.answer.text: The Nairobi River is real. Trade between Kikuyu and Maasai people is documented. These two women, this bargain and the bead are invented. We are imagining one meeting, not retelling a family memory.

q.e1.trust.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.trust.answer.text: Because Naserian remembers being the one who needed time. Today she chooses to wait for Wambui. That choice belongs to these fictional women; it is not a rule about either community.

q.today.who.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.today.who.answer.text: This particular garden and its gardeners are imagined. It lets us ask what a memory from the earlier story might mean in a place people share today.
